# sanitize_filenames

[← Command index](README.md)

Rename files so their names are plain ASCII and safe on every filesystem.

## Synopsis

```
sanitize_filenames [options]
```

## Description

Renames each file directly inside the input directory. Accented and other non-ASCII
characters are transliterated to ASCII (`Pokémon` becomes `Pokemon`) or dropped, the
characters `< > : " / \ | ? *` and control characters are removed, trailing spaces and
dots are stripped, and runs of spaces collapse to one.

Subdirectories and the files inside them are not touched.

## Options

### General

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `-i, --input_path <input_path>` | Directory whose top-level files are renamed; it must exist. |

### Common options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `-v, --verbose` | Enable verbose mode. |
| `-p, --pretend_run` | Do a pretend run with no permanent changes. |
| `-x, --exit_on_failure` | Enable exit on failure mode. |
| `--no-preview` | Skip the preview confirmation prompt. |

## Examples

### Sanitize the names of files in a directory

```bash
sanitize_filenames -i ~/Downloads/Soundtrack
```

### Preview the renames without the confirmation prompt

```bash
sanitize_filenames -i ~/Downloads/Soundtrack -p -v --no-preview
```

## Notes

- If the cleaned name is already taken, that file is left with its old name.
- It stops at the first rename that fails.
